open.fix: USE THE THEOREMS. 82 of 190 tools carry honest-scope PROSE totalling 23,282 bytes (~5,821 tokens), and 110 tools ALREADY cite a sealed theorem — the pattern exists and is simply not applied to scope. A theorem key costs ~6 tokens; a scope sentence averages ~71. Replacing the prose with a citation is ~12x cheaper AND strictly more honest, because a cited theorem is VERIFIED scope where prose only asserts it. That is this project law already: cite a sealed theorem or the claim is UNVERIFIED. So the catalogue carries one sentence on what the tool does plus the keys it is bounded by, and a client that wants the reasoning fetches the theorem — which it can then recompute. This supersedes the earlier cap-at-200-bytes fix: capping DELETES the scope, citing PROVES it.
open.caution: The earlier caution stands but inverts: do not delete scope prose to save tokens. Replace it with the theorem that seals the same bound, which is smaller AND checkable. Where no theorem seals a stated bound, that is a finding in itself — a scope claim with nothing behind it.

open.what: The statement is (2:Nat)^2 < 2^3 and 2^3 = 8 — that is, 4 < 8. Squaring is the RIGHT way to bracket the Tsirelson bound 2*sqrt2 without an irrational, since its square is 8 against the classical 4. But the arithmetic only asserts two numbers are ordered. It derives neither bound, computes no correlator, and names no measurement setting, while the prose says quantum correlations exceed every local hidden variable. Not vacuous — change the numbers and it fails — but the framing reaches past what the statement establishes, the same class as hardware_above_landauer.
open.reproduce: read the statement beside its why: the why describes CHSH, the Lean says 4 < 8
open.fix: Either derive it or say plainly that it is a BRACKET on two published bounds rather than a derivation. A full CHSH correlator needs measurement angles and therefore cosines, which are irrational, and Math.* is rejected tree-wide — so the reduction to squared bounds is a legitimate consequence of this ledger honest constraints, not laziness. The honest form states that constraint in the why. What COULD be derived in exact integers: that the Bell state distribution [1,0,0,1]/2 gives perfect correlation while any product state cannot, which is the no-hidden-variable content reachable without trigonometry.
open.caution: Do not delete it. The squared bracket is the correct idiom for an irrational bound and matches caesium_light_step. The defect is the prose claiming a derivation, not the arithmetic.

open.where: agent orchestration, not the codebase - recorded here because it is the largest measured token sink of the session
open.what: A DELEGATING AGENT THAT WAITS ON CHILDREN CAN BURN ITS ENTIRE BUDGET REPORTING THAT IT IS WAITING. One research agent spawned three sub-researchers, then emitted eight completion notifications of roughly 110k tokens each - about 800k tokens - every one saying only that it was still waiting. Its children had ALREADY completed and reported directly to the parent session, so it was blocked on work that had finished. TaskStop reports it as completed at each notification, so there is no live process to kill: each cycle finishes and respawns a wait.
open.reproduce: compare the sub-agent completion notifications, which carried full findings, against the parent agent notifications over the same window, which carried none
open.fix: Do not have an agent delegate and then wait. Either it does the work, or it spawns children that report to the ROOT session directly - which is what actually happened here and is what delivered. The parent added a waiting loop and nothing else. Where a fan-out is genuinely needed, the root should spawn the children itself.
open.caution: The research itself was NOT wasted - the children produced the sessions best work, including six refutations of widely cited claims and one self-caught fabrication. The waste is entirely in the coordination layer, so the lesson is about orchestration shape and not about delegation being unproductive.

The js mirror is what makes each fact falsifiable — emit() checks every predicate before a byte is written — and the mirror needs the fact expressed in TypeScript BEFORE the .lean exists. open.what: A FIX INSTRUCTION THAT FAILS WHEN FOLLOWED — five places prescribe `npm run gen:packages`, and package.json carries no such script (it exits with npm's 'missing script' error). Found by following the guard's own exact fix after a package surface drifted: the guard reported the drift correctly, named the command, and the command did not exist. The repair is real and one line away — `node dist/scripts/gen-packages.js` is what develop.ts's CURES table already runs for this exact drift, and `npm run x -- gen-packages` is what the scripts law now prescribes in place of thin wrappers, since the dispatcher discovers every script. Not repaired in this session because all five sites sit in files another process is actively writing (guard.ts, one-receipt.ts and mcp.ts were each modified within minutes of the measurement), and editing a file mid-write is how a corrupted snapshot gets attributed to the wrong author.
open.why: The guard's value is that its fix is exact — a gap it names is meant to be closeable by pasting the line it prints. A fix text that fails teaches the reader to distrust the whole class, and it is the one kind of defect the guard cannot catch about itself: nothing checks that a prescribed npm script exists. The same check is cheap to compute — every `npm run <name>` appearing in a fix string must be a key of package.json's scripts — which is exactly the shape of guard finder that would stop this returning.
open.fix: replace `npm run gen:packages` with `npm run x -- gen-packages` in all five sites, then add a finder (one-receipt or guard) that scans fix strings for `npm run <name>` and objects when <name> is not a key of package.json scripts — the computed guard that prevents the class, not just this instance.
